text.en: A shaving mirror makes your face look bigger and a car's rear-view mirror shows a wide road. Curved mirrors bend light differently.

Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
A spherical mirror is curved. A concave mirror curves inward and a convex mirror curves outward.
Terms: pole P, centre of curvature C, principal axis, principal focus F and focal length f. For a spherical mirror, f = R/2.
A concave mirror forms real and inverted images, except when the object is between P and F, where the image is virtual, erect and enlarged.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, behind the mirror.
Sign convention: distances measured from the pole; to the right is positive and to the left is negative. Heights above the axis are positive.
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u.
Uses: concave mirrors in torches, shaving mirrors and dentists' mirrors; convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors because they give a wider field of view.

problem.en: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the image position.

text.en: v = -30 cm. The image is real, inverted and at the same distance (object at C).

prompt.en: How do spherical mirrors form images and what formulas do we use?

points.en: Concave mirrors form real inverted or virtual enlarged images.
Convex mirrors always form virtual, erect, diminished images.
